condition_entries.name: Possible poisoning (toxic food, medicine or chemical)

red_flags.description: Seizures, trembling, collapse or difficulty breathing
Repeated vomiting, drooling, a racing heart or restlessness after eating chocolate
Weakness, wobbly walking or collapse after sugar-free gum, sweets or baking containing xylitol
Bleeding from the gums or nose, blood in urine or faeces, bruising, pale gums or breathlessness, which can appear 3 to 5 days after rat poison
Acting drunk, drinking a lot or vomiting after possible access to antifreeze or screen wash

condition_entries.prevention_tips: Keep chocolate, sugar-free sweets and gum, grapes, raisins, onions, garlic and all human and pet medicines shut away, out of reach and out of handbags. Store rat and slug poison, antifreeze and garden or cleaning chemicals in sealed containers where pets cannot reach them, and mop up spills straight away. Never give your pet human painkillers. Save your vet's out-of-hours number and an animal poison helpline in your phone. If it happens: phone your vet or a poison helpline straight away, do not make your pet vomit unless a vet tells you to, and take the packaging or a sample with you.
possible_causes: Chocolate: dark and baking chocolate and cocoa are the most dangerous; signs can take several hours to appear
Xylitol (birch sugar) and some other sweeteners in sugar-free gum, sweets, peanut butter and baking: can cause a dangerous drop in blood sugar within an hour and liver damage in dogs
Grapes, raisins, sultanas and currants, including in cakes and hot cross buns: even small amounts can cause kidney failure
Onions, garlic, leeks and chives, including powders and cooked food: damage red blood cells, often a few days later
Human medicines such as paracetamol, ibuprofen and other anti-inflammatories: a single tablet can be dangerous, and paracetamol is especially toxic to cats
Rat and mouse poison: many types stop the blood clotting, with bleeding appearing days later
Antifreeze and screen wash (ethylene glycol): sweet-tasting and quickly causes kidney failure; treatment is only effective if started within hours
Many poisons cause no signs for hours or days, so waiting to see if your pet seems unwell is not safe
recommended_examinations: Phone ahead so the clinic can prepare, and take the packaging, label or a sample of what was eaten
Your vet may safely make your pet vomit if it is early enough and appropriate: do not try this at home
Activated charcoal, intravenous fluids and monitoring, depending on the poison
Blood and urine tests to check the kidneys, liver, blood sugar and blood clotting
Specific antidotes where they exist, for example vitamin K after rat poison

condition_entries.name: Lily or permethrin poisoning in cats

red_flags.description: Any contact with a lily, even pollen on the fur or a sip of vase water, before signs appear
Vomiting, drooling, hiding or not eating after contact with a lily
Peeing much more, or much less or not at all, in the days after lily contact
Twitching, tremors, wobbliness or seizures after a flea or tick product, or after contact with a recently treated dog

condition_entries.prevention_tips: Do not keep lilies (Lilium) or day lilies (Hemerocallis) in a home with a cat, and check bouquets before bringing them in. Only use flea and tick products made for cats, and keep cats away from dogs treated with permethrin products for as long as the label says. If a dog product has been put on your cat, phone your vet at once; they may advise washing it off with a mild washing-up liquid and lukewarm water, keeping your cat warm afterwards.
possible_causes: Lilies (Lilium) and day lilies (Hemerocallis): every part is toxic to cats, including pollen groomed off the fur and the water in the vase, and can cause kidney failure within 1 to 3 days
Permethrin in spot-ons, sprays or collars made for dogs: cats cannot break it down, so a dog product put on a cat, or close contact with a recently treated dog, can cause tremors and seizures
Human painkillers, especially paracetamol, which is highly toxic to cats
recommended_examinations: Take the plant, flower or product packaging with you
Early decontamination by your vet, such as safe vomiting after a lily or bathing off a flea product
Intravenous fluids for at least 48 hours after lily exposure, with blood tests to monitor the kidneys
Medicines to control tremors or seizures, and careful temperature monitoring

condition_entries.name: Not eating or low energy in dogs

red_flags.description: Collapse, inability to stand, difficulty breathing, or pale, grey or yellow gums
A swollen, tight belly with retching that brings nothing up
Not eating for more than 24 hours in a puppy, or for more than 2 days in an adult dog
Not eating alongside vomiting, diarrhoea or refusing water

condition_entries.prevention_tips: Know what is normal for your dog: how much they eat and drink and how active they are. Keep bins, bones, toys and socks out of reach, keep vaccinations and parasite control up to date, and change food gradually over about a week.
possible_causes: Stomach upset, often after eating something unusual, or a change of food
Dental pain or a sore mouth
Pain elsewhere, for example from the joints or back
A swallowed object blocking the gut
Infections, fever, or illness affecting the kidneys, liver or pancreas
Poisoning
Stress, heat, or a recent vaccination or medication
recommended_examinations: A full physical exam, including the mouth, belly and temperature
Blood and urine tests
X-rays or ultrasound of the belly if a blockage is possible

condition_entries.name: Not eating or low energy in cats (risk of fatty liver)

red_flags.description: Not eating for more than 24 hours: cats can quickly develop serious liver problems (hepatic lipidosis), especially if overweight
Yellow tinge to the gums, skin or the whites of the eye (jaundice)
Collapse, hiding and not moving, open-mouth breathing, or pale or grey gums
Straining in the litter tray with little or no urine

condition_entries.prevention_tips: Notice early when your cat eats less, especially if they are overweight. Never put a cat on a strict diet or make sudden food changes: weight loss should be gradual and planned with your vet. Keep string, ribbon, thread and hair ties out of reach.
possible_causes: Fatty liver (hepatic lipidosis), which can develop after only a few days without food
Dental disease or mouth pain
Kidney disease, pancreatitis, an overactive thyroid or other illness
A swallowed object, especially string or thread
Infections and fever
Stress, such as a house move, a new pet or a food change
recommended_examinations: A full physical exam, including the mouth, weight and temperature
Blood tests, including liver and kidney values
Abdominal ultrasound or X-rays
Assisted feeding, sometimes through a feeding tube, if your cat has stopped eating

condition_entries.name: Coughing in dogs (kennel cough, airway or heart disease)

red_flags.description: Struggling to breathe, fast breathing at rest, or blue, grey or pale gums or tongue
Sudden coughing and gagging after chewing or playing, as if something is stuck
Coughing up blood, or fainting
Cough with tiredness, poor appetite or a fever (possible pneumonia)
Cough that is worse at night or at rest in a dog with a heart murmur

condition_entries.prevention_tips: Keep your dog's vaccinations up to date, including kennel cough if they meet other dogs, go to kennels or classes. Use a harness rather than a collar for dogs that cough, avoid smoke and dusty air, and keep your dog a healthy weight. Ask your vet to check older dogs' hearts regularly. Dogs with kennel cough are infectious, so keep them away from other dogs until your vet says otherwise.
possible_causes: Kennel cough (infectious tracheobronchitis): a harsh, honking cough, often after contact with other dogs
Something stuck in the throat or airway, such as a grass seed or stick fragment
Heart disease causing fluid in the lungs, often with a cough at night and tiring easily
Collapsing windpipe in small breeds, often a 'goose-honk' cough when excited or pulling on the lead
Pneumonia, chronic bronchitis or lungworm
recommended_examinations: Listening to the heart and lungs
Chest X-rays
Heart scan (echocardiogram) if heart disease is possible
A test for lungworm, or airway samples if the cough is long-lasting

condition_entries.name: Coughing in cats (often asthma)

red_flags.description: Open-mouth breathing or panting, fast breathing at rest, or blue, grey or pale gums
Crouching low with the neck stretched out and struggling to breathe (possible asthma attack)
Coughing up blood, or collapse
Cough with tiredness, not eating or a fever

condition_entries.prevention_tips: A cough in a cat is never normal and is often mistaken for hairballs, so have it checked. Avoid smoke, scented sprays, plug-in air fresheners and dusty or scented cat litter. Keep worming up to date, including lungworm if your cat hunts. If your cat has asthma, give medicines exactly as prescribed and ask your vet for a plan for attacks.
possible_causes: Feline asthma or chronic bronchitis: the most common reason cats cough
Hairballs, though a cat bringing up hair usually retches rather than coughs
Lungworm or other parasites
Respiratory infections
Heart disease or a growth in the chest, especially in older cats
Something inhaled, such as a grass blade
recommended_examinations: Listening to the chest and checking breathing rate
Chest X-rays
A faecal test for lungworm
Airway samples (bronchoalveolar lavage) in some cases

condition_entries.name: Eye problems (conjunctivitis, ulcers and injuries)
breed_predispositions: flat-faced (brachycephalic) breeds such as Pugs, Shih Tzus and Persians

red_flags.description: An eye injury, or an eyeball that is bulging or has come out of its socket
An eye that suddenly turns cloudy, blue or looks bigger than the other
Chemicals splashed into the eye, or sudden loss of sight
Squinting, keeping the eye shut, or pawing or rubbing at it (possible ulcer)
The third eyelid showing, or pupils of different sizes

condition_entries.prevention_tips: Keep long hair trimmed away from the face, and check the eye area daily in flat-faced breeds. Do not let dogs travel with their head out of the car window. Never use human eye drops or old medicines on your pet's eye: some can make ulcers much worse. If chemicals get into the eye, rinse gently with plenty of clean, lukewarm water and phone your vet. Stop your pet rubbing the eye on the way to the vet.
possible_causes: Conjunctivitis from allergies, infection (such as cat flu) or irritants
A scratch or ulcer on the surface of the eye
Something in the eye, such as a grass seed
Dry eye (low tear production), common in some dog breeds
Eyelid problems such as eyelids or lashes rubbing on the eye
Glaucoma (raised pressure inside the eye) or inflammation inside the eye (uveitis)
recommended_examinations: An eye exam with a bright light, checking under the eyelids for foreign bodies
Fluorescein stain to look for ulcers
Tear test (Schirmer tear test)
Eye pressure measurement

condition_entries.name: Ear problems (infection, mites or grass seeds)
breed_predispositions: dogs with floppy or hairy ears, such as Spaniels

red_flags.description: Head tilt, loss of balance, walking in circles, or flickering eye movements
Sudden, violent head shaking after a walk in long grass (possible grass seed)
An ear that is very painful, bleeding, or makes your pet cry when touched
An ear flap swollen like a soft balloon (aural haematoma)

condition_entries.prevention_tips: Check your pet's ears weekly and after walks in long grass, especially in summer, and keep the fur between the toes and around the ears trimmed. Only clean ears with a cleaner your vet recommends, never with cotton buds pushed into the canal, and dry them after swimming. Treat all pets in the house if ear mites are found. Ongoing ear problems are often linked to allergies, so ask your vet about the cause.
possible_causes: Outer ear infection (otitis externa) with bacteria or yeast, often linked to allergies
Ear mites, especially in kittens, puppies and pets from multi-animal homes; very itchy, with dark, crumbly wax
A grass seed or other object in the ear canal
An aural haematoma: a blood blister in the ear flap caused by shaking
Middle or inner ear infection, polyps or growths, which can affect balance
recommended_examinations: Looking down the ear canal with an otoscope, sometimes under sedation
Examining a swab of ear wax under the microscope (cytology) for mites, yeast and bacteria
A full neurological check if balance is affected

condition_entries.name: Constipation

red_flags.description: Straining in the litter tray with little or no urine, especially in a male cat: a blocked bladder can look like constipation
A swollen or painful belly
No poo for more than 48 hours
Vomiting, not eating or lethargy alongside straining
Blood, string or another object visible at the bottom: do not pull it out

condition_entries.prevention_tips: Make sure fresh water is always available (wet food and water fountains help cats drink more), keep your pet active and a healthy weight, and do not feed cooked bones. Keep litter trays clean and easy to reach for older cats with stiff joints. Groom long-haired pets regularly to reduce swallowed hair. Do not give human laxatives or enemas: some are toxic to pets.
possible_causes: Dehydration or not drinking enough
Eating bones, hair, grass or other indigestible material
Pain when squatting, from arthritis, anal gland problems or injury
Kidney disease or megacolon (an enlarged, weak bowel), especially in older cats
A blockage in the gut, or an enlarged prostate in older male dogs
Lack of exercise or a dirty or hard-to-reach litter tray
recommended_examinations: A physical exam, including feeling the belly and a rectal exam
Checking the bladder, to rule out a urinary blockage
X-rays of the belly
Blood tests, especially in older cats

condition_entries.name: Heatstroke (overheating)
breed_predispositions: flat-faced (brachycephalic) breeds such as Bulldogs, Pugs and Persian cats

red_flags.description: Heavy panting or noisy breathing that does not settle with rest in a cool place; any panting in a cat
Bright red, pale or grey gums, or thick drool
Vomiting, diarrhoea, wobbliness, confusion, collapse or seizures

condition_entries.prevention_tips: Never leave a pet in a car, conservatory or caravan on a warm day, even for a few minutes. Walk dogs in the cool early morning or late evening, avoid hot pavements, and skip exercise on hot days for flat-faced, overweight, old or heart-affected pets. Always provide shade, fresh water and a cool place to rest. First aid if it happens: move your pet into shade or a cool room, pour cool (not ice-cold) water over them, use a fan, offer small sips of water, and go to the vet straight away, keeping the car cool on the way. Do not cover your pet with a wet towel, which traps heat.
possible_causes: Being left in a hot car, conservatory or other enclosed space
Exercise or play in warm or humid weather
No access to shade or water
Flat-faced breeds, overweight, very young or old pets, and pets with heart or airway disease overheat more easily
Heatstroke can damage the brain, kidneys, gut and blood clotting even when a pet seems to recover
recommended_examinations: Temperature monitoring while your pet is cooled safely
Intravenous fluids and oxygen
Blood tests for organ damage and blood clotting
Monitoring in hospital for at least 24 hours, because complications can appear later

condition_entries.name: Bloat and twisted stomach (GDV)

red_flags.description: Retching or trying to vomit but bringing nothing up, or only froth
A swollen, tight or drum-like belly
Restlessness, pacing, drooling, pale gums, fast breathing, weakness or collapse

condition_entries.prevention_tips: For large, deep-chested dogs: feed two or three smaller meals a day instead of one large meal, avoid exercise for about an hour before and after eating, slow down fast eaters, and do not use raised food bowls unless your vet advises them. Ask your vet about a preventive gastropexy (stomach-tacking) operation, often done at the same time as neutering. Know where your nearest out-of-hours vet is.
possible_causes: Gastric dilatation: the stomach fills with gas, food or fluid
Volvulus: the swollen stomach twists, cutting off its blood supply and that of the spleen; this can kill within hours
Higher risk in large, deep-chested breeds, older dogs, dogs eating one large meal a day or eating quickly, and dogs with a close relative who had bloat
recommended_examinations: Emergency X-rays to check whether the stomach has twisted
Releasing gas from the stomach, intravenous fluids and pain relief
Emergency surgery to untwist the stomach and fix it in place (gastropexy)
Heart rhythm monitoring after treatment
